query: An FeCoNiCrAl high-entropy-alloy bond coat deposited from 15–45 μm feedstock does not attain the required coating thickness. For thermal-spray deposition and subsequent service as a bond coat in a thermal barrier coating system, what single intervention could overcome this thickness shortfall while preserving coating integrity and minimal as-sprayed oxidation? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, the predicted outcome relative to the 15–45 μm-feedstock baseline, the operating and service conditions under which it should remain effective, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled experiment with a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: Integrating a local inert gas shrouding system into the HVOF spray process will enable a reduced stand-off distance that boosts particle kinetic energy and deposition efficiency, thereby increasing the coating thickness achieved with 15–45 μm FeCoNiCrAl feedstock, while the inert atmosphere minimizes extra in-flight oxidation.
generation.material_initial_state: Gas-atomized FeCoNiCrAl high-entropy alloy powder with a particle size range of 15–45 μm.
generation.intervention: Implement a localized inert gas (e.g., argon) shrouding system around the spray nozzle, allowing the operator to safely reduce the stand-off distance.
generation.conditions: Performed during HVOF thermal-spray deposition with a reduced spray distance under a controlled inert shroud; typical substrate temperatures and ambient pressures as in standard deposition, but with local oxygen exclusion.
generation.structural_mediator: Enhancement of particle kinetic energy at impact (due to reduced stand-off distance) combined with suppressed oxidation on particle surfaces (due to inert gas shrouding) leads to improved splat flattening and coating build‐up.
generation.mechanism: Lowering the spray distance increases particle momentum, improving flattening and deposition efficiency; however, normally this also elevates oxidation. The inert shrouding minimizes oxygen exposure during flight, maintaining the integrity of the particles and preventing excessive oxidation while still promoting a denser, thicker deposit.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline process without shrouding, the modified process will yield a significantly thicker bond coat (improved deposition efficiency) with similar or lower as-sprayed oxide levels, thus preserving coating integrity and adhesion.
generation.baseline: Conventional HVOF deposition without inert shrouding using 15–45 μm powder at a standard stand-off distance, which results in a coating thickness shortfall (insufficient thickness) with minimal oxidation.
generation.boundary: This intervention is expected to be effective only if the shrouding system reliably excludes ambient oxygen and does not introduce turbulent flow that might disrupt particle trajectories; extreme deviations in particle morphology or ambient conditions could reduce its effectiveness.
generation.uncertainty: This hypothesis combines findings that reduced stand-off distances can improve particle kinetic energy and deposition efficiency (PMC10820071, evidence on spray distance effects) with literature on controlling in-flight oxidation via inert environments (PMC8875499 and related studies). The precise balance between kinetic enhancement and oxidation control using inert shrouding in FeCoNiCrAl has not been directly established, making the optimal shrouding parameters an open question.

falsification_experiment.design: Conduct a comparative HVOF deposition study on FeCoNiCrAl coatings using the 15–45 μm feedstock under two conditions: (a) a standard setup at a conventional stand-off distance without inert shrouding and (b) a modified setup with a reduced stand-off distance enabled by local inert (argon) shrouding. Both sets should be performed under identical substrate and ambient conditions.
measurements: Oxide content and distribution (using XPS/EDS analysis)
Microstructural integrity and porosity (using SEM imaging)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the shrouded, reduced stand-off process does not produce a statistically significant increase in coating thickness while maintaining or lowering oxide content compared to the baseline, or if it leads to degradation of coating adhesion or integrity, then the hypothesis is refuted.

cited_evidence.text: Thus, in-flight oxidation of the AlCoCrFeNi particle during the spraying process can be beneficial for the tribological performance of the HEA coatings. Due to high specific surface area, the powder can oxidize differently from the cast bulk alloy. Moreover, the formation of multiple oxides—alumina, chromia, and spinel—changes the residual particle’s core composition and can lead to phase destabilization. Therefore, understanding the regularity of the oxidation behavior and phase transformation of the high-entropy powder at different conditions should be necessary for the production of a coating with high and determined property levels. In this work, the oxidation behavior and phase transformations of FeNiCoCrMo0.5Al1.3 high-entropy alloy powder, produced via gas atomization, were studied. Powder oxidation and phase transformations were studied under HVOF deposition, during continuous heating, and under prolonged isothermal annealing at 800 °C. FeNiCoCrMo0.5Al1.3 HVOF coatings were produced using various distances from the spray nozzle to the substrate to produce coatings with different oxide contents, and the coatings’ properties were investigated.

As the spraying distance increases, the average thickness of the coatings slightly decreases due to a stronger scattering of the particles on the longer path. An increase in the spraying distance results in an increase in coating porosity. Porosity depends on the temperature and kinetic energy of the particles []. Particles sprayed from a longer distance have a lower kinetic energy when they strike the substrate, which results in increased porosity. High temperatures and exposure to oxygen lead to the in-flight oxidation of particles; the smaller particles undergo more severe oxidation. With an increase in the spraying distance, the particles are exposed to oxygen for a longer time, which leads to an increased content of oxides (Figure 4d). As the particles oxidize with the formation of alumina, BCC solid solution loses aluminum, which is reflected in a decrease in its lattice parameter (Figure 3b).
